claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys increases local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion increases yield strength.
Greater atomic size mismatch reduces ductility relative to alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Alloys in the proposed comparison can be processed into homogeneous, single-phase microstructures.
Adjusting alloy composition can systematically vary atomic size mismatch among constituent elements.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to characterize local lattice distortion.
Atomic-level strain measurements can characterize local lattice distortion.
Enhanced atomic size mismatch creates local stress fields through increased lattice distortion.
Local stress fields impede dislocation motion.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch will have lower ductility than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
A baseline alloy with minimal atomic size differences will have relatively low local lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate in single-phase solid solutions under quasi-static loading at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism may not govern multiphase or precipitation-hardened alloys.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern at elevated temperatures because thermal activation becomes significant.
Microstructural complexities and overlapping strengthening mechanisms can obscure the quantitative relationship between atomic size mismatch and mechanical properties.
TEM measurements of dislocation density and arrangement can assess changes in dislocation behavior.
